A 61-year-old woman with cervical cancer metastatic to paraaortic and left supraclavicular lymph nodes was treated with systemic chemotherapy: paclitaxel and bevacizumab administered for 63 and 36 days before presentation, respectively, each followed the next day by cisplatin. On day 0, she was admitted for marked elevation of liver enzymes: AST 173 U/L, ALT 221 U/L, γ-GTP 2553 U/L, and ALP 5188 U/L. Abdominal ultrasonography showed wall thickening of the extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts and of the gallbladder, with bile-duct strictures and dilatations. Contrast-enhanced CT confirmed wall thickening of both extrahepatic and intrahepatic bile ducts with luminal narrowing and dilation, and gallbladder wall thickening. On day 2, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy and nasobiliary drainage was performed. Biopsy of the common bile duct showed no malignant cells and only modest infiltration of neutrophils; bile cytology was also negative for malignancy. Ursodeoxycholic acid was started on day 6. On day 9, cholangiography via the drainage tube revealed strictures and dilatations with irregular wall contours in the intrahepatic bile ducts of both lobes, whereas extrahepatic bile-duct changes were modest.

He also noted a sporadic clicking and popping sound on the left sternal edge that could be very loud and was audible without a stethoscope; he recorded it on his smartphone. Laboratory studies, including arterial blood gas analysis, complete blood count, C-reactive protein, D-dimer level, and cardiac troponins, were all within normal limits. An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

A woman in her 50s with a history of recent hospitalization for congestive heart failure developed a painful ulceration on the right distal forearm at a previous peripheral intravenous catheter site. The ulceration appeared a few days after discharge. Recent activities included cleaning her fish tank, playing with her pet cat, and gardening in her indoor cactus garden. No recent travel history or immunosuppressive medications were reported. The patient was readmitted for bacterial pneumonia.

The patient had an ulcerated plaque on the right forearm with 2 tender, 1- to 2-cm red nodules in the right antecubital fossa.

- Histopathologic examination (4-mm punch biopsy):  - Showed marked superficial and deep inflammation composed predominantly of neutrophils with associated tissue necrosis  - Multiple filamentous gram-positive bacilli identified on Gram stain  - Ziehl Nielson, Fite, and periodic acid–Schiff stains were negative for organisms  Images:  Image A Title: Ulcerated plaque on the right forearm  Image A Description: Shows ulcerated plaque and 2 tender, 1- to 2-cm red nodules in the right antecubital fossa    Image B Title: Histopathologic examination  Image B Description: Dense neutrophilic infiltrate with associated tissue necrosis (Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20)    Image C Title: Gram stain examination  Image C Description: Organisms seen on Gram stain (Original magnification ×60)  - Tissue culture: Positive for specific organism

A 76-year-old woman with a history of appendicitis, torsion of an ovarian cyst pedicle, and uterine myoma presented with a rapidly enlarging right parietal mass behind the ear over one month. She had no neurological deficits or systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies, including complete blood counts, metabolic panel, and viral serology for HIV and Epstein-Barr virus, were all normal or negative. Noncontrast CT of the head revealed a 5-cm hyperdense meningeal mass with parietal bone invasion. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI showed a heterogeneously enhancing lesion in the right parietal region. Cerebral angiography demonstrated a vascular tumor supplied by the middle meningeal artery. Thus, a clinical diagnosis of osteoblastic meningioma was made, and the differential diagnosis included primary lymphoma, metastasis, and sarcoma. The patient underwent endovascular embolization of the feeding artery followed by surgical resection. Intraoperatively, the tumor was extradural, caused skull destruction, and had no intradural involvement. Histology showed a malignant spindle cell neoplasm with positive immunostaining for α-smooth muscle actin, vimentin, and desmin, and negative staining for Epstein-Barr virus.
